utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jarcevic, you were saying that you travelled to different negotiations and on different occasions. In view of the circumstances, could you travel from any other airport but the Belgrade airport?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, when we visited certain political parties -- these are not really negotiations but this was in Italy, and we travelled from Timisoara in Romania. And I think that twice when we travelled to Moscow we used the Timisoara airport.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off because we cannot hear the speakers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Most often we travelled on UNPROFOR planes, then they took us directly from the Belgrade airport to Geneva. And from Budapest we used a plane to go to the United States via France.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, something doesn't seem to be working here. This installation that usually works --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we have that attended to by the technical staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the interpreters to say something so that I can check whether I can hear them. Yes. Thank you. It works now. All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said a few moments ago. Did you most often travel from Belgrade when you went on these trips?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often from Belgrade, primarily when we were taken by UNPROFOR. But I know that the Republic of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia lent its aircraft to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not important. The point is that you travelled from Belgrade most often in view of the circumstances involved. Did your delegation ever visit me prior to going on some trip when you were all together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually we did not pay any calls on you. I just know that once we came to your office, but several days before we went to the negotiations. We informed you that these negotiations would ensue. This was in March in Geneva. If you wish, I can repeat what we talked about then, the only things we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without going into our platform, because I hadn't even completed the platform for these negotiations yet, you did not really give us any suggestions in view of the methodology of negotiations. You only said a single sentence and that was sign the agreement. Reach an agreement with the Croats so that these children would not be killed at the borders on both sides. Nothing else. I didn't hear anything else from you then although I thought that we would discuss matters and agree on things. This was my first meeting with you before the important business that lay ahead of the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina because international negotiators promised that in Geneva we would reach an agreement that would lead to a final peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. Let us go back to Milan Babic's assertions here. He spoke on the 19th of November, 2002, transcript pages 13065 through 67 and 13501, 14104, 105. Approximately -- well, not approximately, but briefly, what he said that was the official reasons presented in the media in terms of the JNA intervening in order to separate the warring parties and deblocking garrisons, that that was not true and that actually it intervened in order to serve the purposes of my policy. What can you say about that, that the JNA did not intervene in order to separate the warring parties, to deblock the garrisons, but for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at this statement of Mr. Babic, then we have to see what the time is. That was 1991 and parts of 1992, while the Yugoslav People's Army was in the Republic of Serb Krajina. Certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that it was sometime in 1991 when this happened.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to remind you that at that time in 1991 the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in place and that the key positions there were held by the representatives of Croatia and Slovenia, precisely because the top echelons of the Yugoslav People's Army were practically manned by Slovenes and Croats. There's another interesting thing I can tell you here. For example, all ambassadors in Europe were mostly from Croatia and Slovenia, whereas Serbia had its representative only in Great Britain. So you can imagine how this illegal import of weapons into Croatia took place. I'm sure that most of the heads of these embassies and consulates had already been prepared for the secession of their republics from Yugoslavia. The only conclusion that I can draw is that Babic has provided complete misinformation. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please just concentrate on the question and don't digress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said that the structure of the attacks was such that the police and the volunteers of the Krajina would be engaged in provocations and open gunfire individually at Croat settlements, and then the Croats would return fire and then this would give the JNA a pretext to intervene. And as he said, they would do that by using heavy artillery and different units under their command in order to attack Croat towns. Can you say anything about this? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct at all, because the Yugoslav People's Army did not have such assignments at all. It did not attack Croat towns in order to take them or in order to expel the Croat population from them. The only thing it did was protect the Serb people in the remaining part of the former Croatia. And as far as we can see, 400.000 betrayed Serbs had nothing to do with the provocations that Babic is talking about, and yet again they had to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you tell us how, if at all, you became privy to the assignments of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was quite simple. Had the army had the kind of assignments as Babic says, it would have been no problem for them to reach the Italian border. You just have to resort to simple logic, not any special kind of information. The Croatian army was not a daunting force. It could not have stopped the Yugoslav army had it had the kind of assignments that Babic is saying it had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's just a matter of logic and reasoning. You didn't have any specific information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had information as president -- or, rather, as minister in the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina. I know that often we complained about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were a minister of what at the time? Foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say this: As I informed you yesterday, I was foreign minister from October 1992 until April 1994, but I had information about the activities of the Yugoslav People's Army in 1991 in the area of the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic says, on transcript page 13234, that the provisions of the Vance Plan were not observed in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday we touched on that subject, the Vance Plan. The police of the Republic of Serb Krajina was supposed to have revolvers only or the kind of weapons worn on the hip, as defined there. However, there were large-scale aggressions of the Croat army, and Serbs were being disturbed every day across the border, and the police of the Krajina had to keep some automatic weapons. That's why Babic said that the Vance Plan had not been fully observed. And on the other hand, there was no peace, and that was a requirement of the Vance Plan, but Babic doesn't say a word about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said that what was prevented was the return of Croats and that Milosevic implicitly supported that, and so on and so forth. Do you know anything about this kind of prevention of the return of Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I know a great deal. That is Resolution 762, which was passed in 1992. And that was the first one that referred to the return of Croats to the Republic of Serb Krajina. And then the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina asked for the Serb people who had been expelled - and there were far many more of them - to receive the same treatment. However, the Security Council remained silent on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said in -- on transcript page 12991, that the army of Republic of Serb Krajina was dependent on the army of Yugoslavia. Do you know anything about that? He claims that I appointed commanders. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I was a member of the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina, the relations between the Republic of Serb Krajina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had all the characteristics of relations between any two countries. Of course, bearing in mind the specific situation involving a total blockade on the part of the rest of the world, and that is the situation that both countries had to face, so military cooperation, police cooperation, industry, economic relations; all of that was involved. I would like to make you aware of yet another fact: Mr. Babic is objecting in terms of some relations that our army had with the army of Yugoslavia. However, we had relations in other fields as well. For example, the weather forecasters who were working in Knin tried to get information in Zagreb. The -- and the people from Zagreb, the Croats, did not even send these people their salaries. So then their weather station had to link itself up to Belgrade, and that is how they received their salaries. Then engineers, electrical engineers, everything had to go on functioning. It was only right for that to happen, because otherwise the population of the Krajina would face its death. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Slobodan Lazarevic testified here. Do you know Slobodan Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know him. He stated here on transcript page 12310 and 309 that he talked to Dusan Rakic and Goran Hadzic before the conference in Norway, and that on that occasion they said to him that allegedly "The Boss" - and they meant me by that - gave them direct and explicit orders not to get anything done at that meeting. Tell me now, were you at that meeting? Did you have this kind of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not at this meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not either. No, no. He wasn't either. He says that Hadzic and Rakic said to him that they had been with me and that I told them that they shouldn't get anything done in Norway. That's what I said to them before they went to Norway.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I started my answer right. I was not at the meeting with you and Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Rakic never told me that they had a meeting with you or that they did not have a meeting with you. I spoke about this yesterday. I talked about the secret negotiations in Norway. Our delegation, according to the draft that was offered by Vollebaek and that Croatia agreed on, our delegation was prepared to sign this agreement. So no one was exercising any influence over us, including you, because we are not the party that refused to sign the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are not the party that refused to sign the agreement. You wanted to sign the agreement. That is what you know from Norway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And he stated here that before every peace conference he and others who took part in peace conferences would get together in Belgrade in order to get instructions from the Serbian government in the following way: The head of delegation would go to see me, and every representative from the delegation would meet with the Serb and federal representatives of the other side. Somebody would meet up with people from my office, allegedly, and others would meet up with other people, and so on and so forth. Was that the way it was? Was that the way this witness described it? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of all the negotiations, none of this happened. I was the one who prepared the platforms, as I explained to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in all the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I participated in the most important ones. The only delegation I was not part of was the one that was supposed to negotiate in Topusko sometime in late 1993. These negotiations, however, fell through because the Croats launched untruths and said that it was the Serb side that was rejecting negotiations. After that, the meeting in Norway followed, and this always happened at the proposal of international mediators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This meeting in Topusko was supposed to take place on the territory of the Krajina, somewhere in the border belt. Is that where Topusko is? Could you explain where it is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topusko is in Kordun province, 30 kilometres, as the crow flies, from Zagreb. The Croats agreed to go there but then they had a change of heart, obviously, and found a pretext which was not based in fact because Djordje Bjegovic, the Prime Minister, said that they were about half an hour late and that the Croats used this as an excuse to tell their own public that the Serbs were not cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness claims that during those meetings Goran Hadzic spoke to the president of the SRJ, Zoran Lilic, and then that he spoke in the course of the meetings, depending on the topic, with the Chief of the General Staff Perisic, or with Stanisic. Tell us, please, whether this was Slobodan Lazarevic's position and that he had this kind of information available even had it happened.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, President Hadzic never informed the government of any visit of that kind or of any kind of conclusions reached with the leadership of the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the police leaders. At cabinet sessions we never received any such reports. Mr. Lazarevic could not have been privy to what the government and the president were doing because his headquarters was in Topusko. If we look at the size of the Republic of Serb Krajina and Croatia, it's far away from Knin and very far away from the headquarters of Mr. Hadzic, who was on the western borders of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about Lazarevic's activities in Topusko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him at the Kordun Corps, and he was introduced to me as the corps interpreter. He was interpreting for our officers who didn't speak any foreign languages in contacts with the UNPROFOR commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lazarevic also testified about what he observed when travelling in the direction of Knin. That's on the 29th of October, 2002, when he testified about that, when he was travelling towards Knin where barricades had been set up along the road during the so-called log revolution, and he saw many cars with Serb licence plates, non-local licence plates, which strengthened his conviction that what he thought had been a spontaneous revolution of the local Serbs was in fact something organised from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's right in one thing, Mr. President: Half of Serbia was in Dalmatia and those areas at the time because it was summertime, and you know that people in Serbia took their vacations and spent their holidays in that part of Yugoslavia. In 1991, Serbs or people from Serbia still used those roads to go for their holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about any involvement of citizens of Serbia in the setting up of roadblocks? This was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For heaven's sake, was any kind of impulse or incentive needed from abroad to get people to defend their homes and their families? I will read some excerpts from Croatian newspapers at the time, and you will see that in many towns Serb houses were being blown up, looted, or set fire to, as were Serbian shops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we want to hear what the Serb peoples had to say on this. The question was what do you know about any involvement of citizens of Serbia in the setting up of roadblocks, but you have gone off on a tangent, as usual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise if I'm doing that. Barricades were not a result of any kind of influence from Serbia. I think I've been clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't -- that wasn't it. The question was the involvement of the citizens of Serbia in the setting up of roadblocks, not influence. Are you saying that there were no citizens of Serbia involved in setting up of roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't. That can't be checked. Even today it's impossible to check that. I said that 2 million people in Serbia originated from that area. Perhaps somebody was visiting his own brother and helped him to do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you visit any of the roadblocks personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I didn't say that. I was in Greece, in Thessaloniki, from April until September 1991, serving there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... speak with confidence as to the involvement of citizens of Serbia in the roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have met many people who did participate in setting up the roadblocks. Mostly they were local people, from the area where the roadblocks were set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The witness stated here that on numerous occasions packages sent from Serbia to the Krajina, or shipments, contained weapons and military equipment, but they were mislabelled as humanitarian aid. Could this witness have informed himself about weapons and equipment being sent as humanitarian aid? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I can't say whether his information was correct or whether he was simply deceiving this Court, but I have met many officers who spoke in similar terms about humanitarian aid, and that was in the UNPROFOR offices organisation. Through the Krajina and Bosnian Krajina they sent weapons to the Muslims in Bihac and even sold weapons to Croatian units. I can give you the name of the man who completed a study on this. He was a colonel. The Court may summon him, if it likes. He was in the army of Republika Srpska, a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. Nikola Samardzic testified here. On page 11428 and 429 of the transcript, Samardzic says that the goal of the JNA was to take Slavonia and Western Srem and arrive at the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before you reply to my question, Mr. Robinson, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that what is called the log revolution happened in 1990, not in 1991, when he was in Greece, as he said, from April to September, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was as follows: Samardzic says that the goal of the JNA was to take the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Do you know what the goal of the army was and if that was the goal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that similar statements were nonsense. Had such a plan existed, it would have been implemented. The Croatian para-army could not have prevented the JNA from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Petar Kriste stated here - that's transcript 14837 to 92 - that Dubrovnik was attacked with the aim of creating a Greater Serbia and taking territory and not, as he said, in order to preserve the constitutional order. What do you think about this statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this statement is just like the previous one. Had this been the plan, there would have been no problems for the JNA in taking Dubrovnik. There were many politicians who were in favour of something like that, because from the earliest times in history Dubrovnik has been a Serbian town. Even today the Croatian language is not spoken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We won't go into historical explanations now, but was it the goal to take Dubrovnik in order to create a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the goal. Had this been the goal, it would have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not a member of any party but that you knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask you, what was the goal, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me? Excuse me, please. I apologise. The goal was as in any place where people were threatened in Yugoslavia; to protect the Serbian people. You know that about 2.200 Serbs were expelled from Dubrovnik before these battles that are mentioned here so often, and all of Western Herzegovina in the hinterland of Dubrovnik had been cleansed of Serbs. The Croatian army there razed to the ground an Orthodox monastery dating from the 14th century. Monasteries like this cannot be found anywhere else in Western Europe. And this was part of the goal to stop the army at the coast; and behind that line, the Serbs inhabited the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Stjepan Mesic, in his statement, said the following: In the beginning when the Serbian Democratic Party was established, it didn't seem that that party would, as he says, become so radical because it was advocating cultural autonomy. However, as time went by, it became clear that this party was being manipulated by Belgrade, which means that the regime of Slobodan Milosevic, and he personally, was manipulating them and they were doing only those things that were leading to the creation of a Greater Serbia, an ethnically pure territory cleansed of the non-Serb population. Tell me, what were the activities of the SDS, and is it correct to say that I manipulated them? Did the SDS leadership maintain any kind of contacts with me? What was that relationship like? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that the two leading men in the SDS, Dr. Raskovic and Dr. Babic, were your political opponents. I don't know why this role is being ascribed to you, of participating in the founding of that party. I'm probably becoming a bit of a bore now, but I have to repeat once again that the setting up of that party was caused by the behaviour of the Croatian political parties and the expulsion of Serbs from the Croatian towns. That this party became more extreme later on than it had been at the beginning is absolutely not correct. In late 1993 and early 1994, new branches of that party emerged, and they participated in the first multi-party democratic elections under the auspices of the Security Council, and two parties came from that first party. One was led by Mr. Babic and the other by Mrs. Solaja, and Babic was elected to parliament. I think he had the majority. As the party was mainly under his leadership, this statement purports to say that he was your man, and I'm saying that he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Mesic said in his statement that in areas where the Serb Democratic Party took power, the population had been fully cleansed of non-Serbs. That's page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard that 189.000 Croats had lived in the Krajina. I don't know how many remained, but I am absolutely sure that the departure of the Croats from the Republic of Srpska Krajina had been organised by the Croatian state in order to create the impression that the Serbs were expelling the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Mesic, in his statement, 10559 - that's the page number - during his cross-examination said that it was an exaggeration to say that there was an atmosphere of fear among the Serbs in Croatia, but he does accept that there were unseemly and unacceptable statements made and that that is a fact. There were also dismissals which were wrong, as he says, but the people who were dismissed were able to file lawsuits and they won their cases. How do you comment on this assessment of the situation in Croatia? Is it true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's completely untrue. Mr. Mesic passed over two facts, and this is something that had never happened anywhere else in the world. The nationality of the Serbs had been taken away from them by decree, which doesn't happen to -- to anyone anywhere else, even if they're criminals. Also, the tenancy rights of the Serbs were rendered null and void. They were not allowed to buy the apartments in which they had tenancy rights, and the homes of those who were expelled were immediately seized and taken away from them. This has never happened anywhere else in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you didn't answer the second part of the question. He explained that the Serbs that were dismissed filed lawsuits and won them. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do know that those lawsuits were filed in recent years but not on a massive scale, not as commensurate with the violations that took place. People have lost their will to do so. And let me tell you, they would take out a permit in Serbia, written in Cyrillic, and the Croatians put it in a drawer and wait until the whole thing is written in the Latin script, which means that there was a great deal of delay, and those lawsuits started just this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesic also said that it was true that there were crimes in Croatia and that he always asked for investigations to be launched and that the perpetrators be brought to justice, but that Croatia didn't have enough legal provisions, and then he won the elections because he wanted to see the rule of law prevail in Croatia. Now, do you know that Croatia didn't have any rules, regulations, things like that, and that investigations were called for into the perpetrators of crimes? Do you know anything about that and may we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say, Mr. President, is to say that I'm surprised to hear that the head of state, even if it is the State of Croatia, should speak in that way. He's a man who could have prevented all those crimes from happening. He was always in the top echelons of the Croatian state, so that command responsibility should be applied to Mr. Mesic in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said that when he was elected to the Presidency he believed and hoped that he would be able to solve the Yugoslav crisis through political means and that he could contribute to avoiding a war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic had a very good chance had he put in prison all the people who imported weapons in 1990 and 1991 in all the different ways that weapons were brought in. Then that wish would have been realised, if that was indeed the wish that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesic says that there were no camps in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right at all. In 1991, at the end of that year, or perhaps it was in 1992, there was an exhibition about the slaughtering of more than a hundred Serbs in Gospic. They were law abiding citizens. Many of them had signed what the Croatian authorities asked them to sign, that is to say -- saying -- writs saying that they were loyal to the Croatian authorities. They were all slaughtered, thrown into pits, as they had been in fascist Croatia in 1941. And furthermore, I can also tell you about the correspondence that I had with the Security Council about a particular camp after which most probably several hundred people were executed in Western Slavonia in a small village there, Marino Selo. And the Security Council -- well, we proposed this investigation and offered to dig up Ovcara. The Security Council gave up the idea because the blame had already been placed squarely -- or, rather, the blame was on the Croatian side rather than on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesic said here that Croatia defended itself because the JNA, under my command, had attacked Croatian territory, and that nobody attacked the barracks but that they were blocked or put under siege to prevent them from being attacked. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's quite nonsensical. I don't know how to describe statements of that kind any more. Millions of people in the world saw the Croats attack the barracks in Split and strangle a young soldier from Macedonia. Now they wish to classify conduct of that kind as an international war. Then it was Croatia and Macedonia who should have been at war, because the first soldier killed was from Macedonia. But all the barracks in Croatia were attacked and, according to UN documents, the attacks on the barracks was termed an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard Ruth Vollebaek here -- Knut Vollebaek, and he said that I exerted pressure on the Serbs in Knin to negotiate with the Croats at his proposal. Do you know anything about that? Just the facts, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President, I didn't understand your question, nor do I know which time frame you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the time that he conducted negotiations with you. And I'm talking about Knut Vollebaek. He said that I had exerted pressure on you for you to agree to negotiate with the Croats at his proposal. So he asked me to prevail upon you to agree to negotiate with the Croats. Now, did you refuse to negotiate at any point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Well, perhaps I'm being too fast for the interpreters, but let me say that Mr. Knut Vollebaek always had open doors for negotiation with the government of Srpska Krajina. I do believe that he went to see you, and he most probably consulted you or informed you of his intentions, and it would be quite mad to suppose that you did not agree to have us negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm interested in an answer to this question: Was there any need for any pressure to be put on you for you to negotiate in view of the fact that your participation in all negotiations or, rather, the Serbian side and leadership in the Serbian regions, did it refuse to negotiate? Did it refuse to have matters settled? Did it refuse any offers that were made, and so on and so forth? What is your experience in view of the fact that you attended all the negotiations except those -- that one set of negotiations in Topusko which were never held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no refusal on our part except for some wavering, and I omitted to say that yesterday, whether to negotiate on Croatian territory or not, but then we agreed to that too and went to Zagreb to negotiate. So we always agreed. It was just in one negotiations when I was not member of the government that there was a condition put on our side, and that was the beginning of 1995, when it was quite obvious that the Security Council would bring in a new Resolution pursuant to which the status of the peace forces in Yugoslavia would be changed, and in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, because up until then they were called the protection force, and we had from Stoltenberg a draft agreement stating that they would lose this status of protection forces but that they would be called something else, forces for boosting confidence or something like that. And this happened at a point when the American Ambassador Galbraith came up with the famous Z-4 plan in Knin. And I already explained that it had been put forward a number of times before that but not under the name of Z-4. And it was not serious, because it related to negotiations between just two towns and the surrounding parts. And Martic said on that occasion, he told the American ambassador that we would negotiate, we would discuss the agreement when the same status was confirmed for United Nations forces as provided by the Vance Plan. However, this was used to put the blame on Martic and say that he was not cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my examination-in-chief of this witness, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you were born in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I said that; on the 2nd of February, 1942.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just answer my question, no additional information is needed. And you -- afterwards, you lived in, in particular in the period we are concerned about, you lived in Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1970, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned already that from April to September 1991 you were in Greece, and my question is before April 1991, where were you? Before Greece, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, I worked in the Foreign Affairs Ministry of the SFRY, in the personnel department.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So you were in Belgrade before April 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And after September 1991, were you in Belgrade or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you stationed after September 1991 in any other country for -- at least for times?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So in relation to the years 1990 to October 1992, you were never in the SAOs in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the years 1990 to your assignment to the RSK in 1992, you never lived in the SAOs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also didn't travel there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. I played at the international chess tournament. Unless I'm very much mistaken, that was in March in 1991 in Pula.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Pula, that's in Croatia. That's not in the SAOs, right? It's not in the SAOs. That's more in --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the SAO, but I was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But in relation to what was going on in the SAOs in that period 1990 to mid-1992, you did not make any direct observations on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know anybody from the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you didn't know anybody from the governments in Knin or in Erdut, you cannot really help us with any -- any observation regarding their relations with Mr. Milosevic or his cabinet or any other government official in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I could. I could not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also cannot help us with matters related to the Serb TOs and police in the Krajina and in Eastern Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the answer was to that question, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Are you saying that you -- you would not be able to be of any assistance in relation to -- to Mr. Milosevic and his cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I said that at that time I didn't know a single leader in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and therefore the fact would emerge that I cannot confirm whether they had any contacts with Mr. Milosevic or what kind at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you did not have any relation with these people in the Krajina or Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, you cannot help us with matters related to their TOs or their police forces either; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking for my assistance, then I can make my conclusions and give you my impressions and the impressions that the inhabitants of Serbia gained at that time, if you're interested in hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I actually asked -- I actually just wanted you to confirm that you cannot really help us there, in relation to the TOs or their subordination or coordination with the JNA and the like. For that period of time, you can't; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that the witness doesn't understand the question properly, because you're using questions like "being of assistance." If you were to ask him whether he knows about it, then he would give you a yes or no answer, but "could you be of assistance," that is not in the spirit of our language and it's difficult for him to understand this expression. If you asked a simple does he know about something, he can say whether he does or not, but "could you be of assistance" and that kind of turn of phrase is difficult for him to understand because, according to what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is saying here, it would appear that the witness knows nothing about anything that went on in Krajina and that he just parachuted into the area like a foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is really putting to you is that you don't have any evidence to give this Court based on your direct knowledge, personal knowledge, in relation to the TOs or their subordination or coordination with the JNA. Do you accept that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you were an official in the SFRY Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as you told us. What did you do in the period from April 1992, when the SFRY did not exist any longer, until October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the Foreign Ministry, occupying the same post that I held beforehand. It was just the circumstances that changed and the structure within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, because the cadres, the personnel from Slovenia and Croatia, started to leave in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. When -- when you became minister of foreign affairs of the RSK in October 1992, did you continue to live in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained that yesterday. I said why.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As I -- if I understand you correctly, you mentioned that the RSK Ministry of Foreign Affairs was actually located in Belgrade. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So even after October 1992, you did not go to Knin or Erdut; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I went, madam. I went officially at least once a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But as you were living in Belgrade, you cannot really tell us, and you cannot -- you do not know what Mr. Lazarevic and the other local -- local officials were doing on a daily basis and with whom they met; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not a clear question at all. I can know what Mr. Lazarevic did at the point in time when I was involved in certain affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Lazarevic when you met him on negotiations and the like, when you went abroad and elsewhere, but you did not observe what he was doing in the region when he met Mr. Hadzic and others. You don't know that because you were not there; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, I said that he lived in Kordun and that Hadzic was a long way away from him and that his affairs in Kordun related to officers, not heads of state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you actually -- you were the liaison person between the RSK and the Belgrade authorities; right? That was your main purpose of your office in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're very wrong on that score, madam. That's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who suggested you for the position, for the RSK position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer that question if the Trial Chamber and Mr. Robinson allow me to explain it, because you can't have a short answer to a question like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Association of Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as I've already said, as we -- I was one of the few babies that survived in my generation. We were very much afraid for the destiny of our people in the Krajina. And what happened once was that a doctor came to see me, Dr. Nikic. He was a man from the neighbouring village next to me. His name was Stanislav Nikic. And he had attended the medical military academy in Belgrade, and he happened to learn that the Croats were preparing to slaughter people in Bosnia and in the place of Livno and a village near Duvno, and he said, "Slobodan, we have to save our people. And this year Portugal is the chair for the European Community, and you have to call up the Portuguese ambassador." At that point in time, many of us Serbs from Bosnia rallied together, and I did indeed call up the ambassador. I'm sorry that I've forgotten his name and surname now, but that was in 1992. And I said, "Mr. Ambassador, the Croatian army, on the basis of our information, is preparing to slaughter a whole village in the Duvno municipality and the village -- name of the village is Rascani." And I said they were also preparing a pogrom and slaughter of the majority population in the town of Livno because the centre of the town of Livno was inhabited by Serbs. And these two municipalities, in the Second World War, were -- 72 per cent were slaughtered during World War II in one of these places and 89 per cent in another. He was very nice, he said just spell out for us the names of those places in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've allowed you to give an answer to the question, not in an abbreviated form, but you are carrying on much too long. Please get to the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did warn you that this would be the point in time when I decided to take up the post of foreign minister of Krajina, because people came to realise this, they saw what was happening, and we saved the people in those parts. And everything -- everybody congratulated me. And the ambassador said, "Mr. Jarcevic, my school friend is the foreign minister of Portugal, and I'll call the ambassador in Zagreb tomorrow, and our ambassador will go and see Tudjman straight away the next day, and he will prevail upon him not to touch those people over there." And that was the decisive moment. And the Serbs who listened to that telephone conversation that I had put me forward for the post of foreign minister. Well, there you have it. It wasn't too long an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you didn't know the people that -- the authorities in the Krajina or in Erdut. They didn't know you either. So my question is: The Serbs -- which Serbs proposed you? Not the ones from the region; right? Other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you; the Serbs from Bosnia, Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you claimed that no Croats were expelled from Serbia or persecuted in Serbia during the events. That's what you said yesterday. And I would like to put to you a report of the UN. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's an exhibit used earlier in these proceedings. It's Exhibit 771. It's in the English language, and we could put it on the ELMO. It's -- please go ahead. I would like to have on the ELMO paragraph 123. It's on page 34. Page 34, paragraph 123.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, this is a report of the General Assembly -- for the General Assembly of the 14th of November, 1992. On page 34, it deals with events in Vojvodina, and it says here in paragraph 123: "The outbreak of fighting --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the picture be improved? Apparently it can't be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I will read parts of it. "The outbreak of fighting in neighbouring parts of Croatia and the influx of Serbian refugees coincided with an increase in incidents of harassment and violence against non-Serbs in Vojvodina, including rape, shootings, death threats, the use of explosives against homes and churches, and forcible eviction." And a little bit further down in that same paragraph, it says: "The report cites the example of Hrtkovci where 500 refugee families, including 350 former servicemen, were resettled in May 1992. A campaign of intimidation and harassment took place, including beatings and culminating in the death of one person and the departure of 600 persons who sought refuge in Croatia." And on the next page, in paragraph 124, it continues: "The town of Novi Slankamen has also been the scene of many violent incidents. A Catholic cultural centre was destroyed and a Roman Catholic Church was damaged in 1991, a number of Croatian homes were damaged by machine-gun fire or explosives, one person was raped, and many others were beaten or threatened. In the city of Sombor, explosives damaged a church on the night of the 31st of December, 1991 - 1 January 1992, and two nights later two Croatian restaurants and the home of a leader of a Croatian political party were damaged by explosives. These crimes were announced on the local radio by the paramilitary leader Arkan. Ethnic Croatians have been told that they must leave by a certain date, under threat of death. In Subotica, where Hungarians are the largest ethnic group, religious sites have been attacked of Hungarians or vandalised repeatedly since 1991. The cathedral was damaged by explosives. An attempt was made to burn a religious school, a monastery in Bac, classified as ..." and so forth and so forth. And it says in the next paragraph: "Local authorities and political leaders who met with the delegation indicated that an estimate of 90.000 Croats and Hungarians and other minorities have fled Vojvodina." Mr. Jarcevic, you were living in Serbia, and so you must know about these events, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I grew up in Vojvodina. I got to Vojvodina when I was age 4, and I am perfectly familiar with the situation in that province. This is my question to your question: The structure of government of the Republic of Serbia did not participate in this. On the contrary, they prevented possible incidents from breaking out and that could have had even worse consequences than the ones that you've been reading about now. Allow me just to say one more thing: Honest people, even from the office in Hrtkovci, gave the authorities of Serbia information to the effect that most of the inhabitants of this village had close cooperation with the HDZ, collected money, and sent that money to arm Croatian paramilitaries. Of course that kind of behaviour caused a reaction on the part of those who were coming in from Croatia as refugees. I believe that the proportions of these crimes are minimal because the organs of Serbia and Yugoslavia managed to stop and prevent what could have happened had it been in the hands of the volunteers and people who had come from Croatia. May I just add one more thing? As opposed to Croatia, where the entire state structure took part in the persecution of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, we also had a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I intervene? The Prosecution took three and a half to four minutes to put that question, which was a very detailed passage from a UN text, probably has very, very marginal relevance to the case in this trial. It's 1992, a report of November 1992. This witness is dealing with Croatia, which is a passage of the indictment from August 1991 to June 1992. We're moving off into Vojvodina. If time is that valuable for the Prosecution, as they continually assert, perhaps we should be dealing with more relevant materials rather than reading out long passages of text and then trying to stop the witness from answering it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. I'll take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why did you raise Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I raised Vojvodina because this witness told us during the examination-in-chief that no Croat was harmed in Serbia and that there was no persecution of Croats in Serbia, and that is not true. And this witness should know it, because he was there, and he actually says he knows very well about Vojvodina. And when we -- when we speak about -- about the importance of these events for the trial, of course the Croatia indictment deals only with the years 1991 and 1992, but this is a joint trial, and how the JCE cooperated throughout the years 1990 to 1999, that's a key issue in this case, and this is what we are also talking about. When we speak about Croatia, it is about the relationships of people spanning the whole period of time. And I will deal -- I will deal with this witness as he does not really know about what was going on in Croatia in 1991 and parts of 1992. I will mostly deal with events that are not in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He did want to add one more thing. What was it that you wanted to say? You indicated earlier that you wanted to say something else, and I'll hear it briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me just repeat: The government structures of Serbia and Yugoslavia were just preventing possible tragedies. It is a sheer miracle that this was not even on a larger scale. Nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We heard that from you already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, we also heard a witness, and it's witness C-047, who were actually in the region, in Vojvodina, during the events, and he told us --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's the witness speaking about Hrtkovci and the other events at T21578, T21641. Basically that's the most parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this witness actually told us that the persecution campaigns in Subotica and Hrtkovci took part after Mr. Vojislav Seselj rallied in these places and that the authorities did not prevent these things from happening. What do you say to this? Is that also what you heard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Seselj did not have any influence over the spread of any kind of crime in Serbia. He was just calling for the defence of the imperiled Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to ask you in relation to another passage of that same report, because you mentioned the media and the role of the media in Serbia. It's again Exhibit 771. Could it be put on the ELMO. And it's page 28, paragraphs 95 and 96. You mentioned, Mr. Jarcevic, in your examination-in-chief that the media in Serbia were rather moderate when they reported about the events in Croatia and elsewhere, and I would like to quote findings from the UN, from the report. It says here in paragraph 95: "The government-controlled electronic media and press have engaged in a one-sided and nationalistic propaganda campaign. The official media have done nothing to distance themselves from the politics of intolerance, and, as a result, have fed the fires of hatred." And a little bit further down, in paragraph 96, it says: "It has been observed that quite often facts are distorted, data falsified, and sometimes atrocities invented or deliberately exposed in order to contribute to an atmosphere of mutual hatred. Media are using offensive and abusive appellations. The activities of various international bodies are presented in a false light, and the atmosphere of siege has been created." And so on. That, Mr. -- What do you say? This is completely different from what you told us, Mr. Jarcevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this report does not correspond to the truth. Could you imagine the expulsion of 400.000 Serbs from Croatia? That was not even registered properly in Serbia. It's only now that people are finding out about this. And what about the UN report? Why did it never provide this kind of information except for Boutros-Ghali's report dated the 15th of May, 1993? And that is a report that was incomplete, at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to that same exhibit, would you please -- Usher, would you please put page 25 on the ELMO. It's paragraph 78. Mr. Jarcevic, you also mentioned the Vance Plan and how the Croatian side violated it, and I would like to put something to you about the Serb side. And as you were at that time already the minister of foreign affairs, you may be able to tell us. It's dealing with Sector South here in this paragraph 78. That's the Knin Krajina. It says here: "In Sector South, part of the so-called 'Republic of Krajina' local authorities practised discrimination." And then further down: "This is of great certain of United Nations staff who collect evidence of murders, robberies, looting, and other forms of criminal violence often related to ethnic cleansing, where in accordance with a mandate, such evidence is transferred to the local authorities. The latter are reluctant to take action if not overtly uncooperative. UNPROFOR officials explained that Serbian militia which were to be disbanded have, in many cases, simply 'changed uniforms,' often working under the auspices of such groups as the Special Police, Border Police, or Multi-purpose Brigades. Until demilitarisation has been completed, UNPROFOR officials believe they cannot guarantee the security either of refugees hoping to return or of the remaining minority populations." Mr. Jarcevic, this is happening now at a time when you were the foreign minister of the RSK. This did happen, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, have I not explained that very nicely? Did I not explain it nicely yesterday? Our police could not have remained without automatic weapons. That is primarily what it has to do about. And we had a meeting with Cyrus Vance in November in Knin, and then Mr. Martic explained that all these units that are mentioned here exist in any other state. In terms of equipping the Ministry of the Interior, we did not really deviate from --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. This paragraph that I read out was only partly about the violation of the Vance Plan regarding demilitarisation. It was also about ethnic cleansing practices conducted by the Serbs. And just to add to this -- Usher, would you please put on the ELMO paragraph 83. That's the next page, related to Sector East, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It says here: "Ethnic cleansing continues to be carried out by militias and local Serbian authorities. The few Croatians, Hungarians, Ukrainians and Slovaks who have not yet left voluntarily are faced with persistent, and often extremely violent, forms of intimidation." The next paragraph: "Catholic churches have been destroyed in an attempt to erase all forms of non-Serbian institutions." Mr. Jarcevic, my question to you is: That's true. Ethnic cleansing took place at that time, and you know about it; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing was not carried out by the organs of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. There were criminals and criminals were prosecuted, for the most part. With the permission of the Chamber, I would like to place a document on the overhead projector where you can see that a man who killed Croats was arrested in Sector South that we have just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be done in re-examination, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would agree with that. If Mr. Milosevic wishes to raise that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to say just his answer to a question. It was a question which had about three questions within it, and he was told off for responding to a different part of the question. He then wants to answer that other question, and he's got a document to prove it. In my submission, he -- with Your Honours' leave, he would be entitled to respond to it in that way and then the Prosecutor has to deal with the information that he is advancing as part of his response. It's for the Prosecutor to then deal with the witness's answer in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll allow you to introduce the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, this is the Territorial Defence of the Republic of the Serb Krajina providing the following information: That on the 17th -- can't really see it; right? I beg your pardon. "On the 11th of March, 1992, in Skabrnja, five locals of Croat ethnicity were killed whereas in Gornja Zemunik four locals also of Croat ethnicity. One person, Maricic Boze Stevo, an ethnic Serb, is suspected of having committed all of this, from Zemunik Gornji. The suspect is a member of the 3rd Brigade of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac. The mentioned person was brought into custody at the public security station in Benkovac. We still do not have information about the names of the victims. The motives for the commission of the crime are still something that we do not know. "Two Catholic churches were destroyed as well in the village of Perusic and Podgradje, the south-eastern part of our municipalities. The churches were almost completely destroyed, and also some graves were demolished." Oh, I thought I was reading slower. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be useful, Mr. Robinson, if this would be on the overhead projector. This document has not been translated previously, and then the interpreters can see what they are interpreting and then the rest of us can have a look as well and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please put it on the overhead projector. Mr. Jarcevic, can you tell us what this document is? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document speaks about crimes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is its official status? Does it have one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a report of the military organs of the Republic of Serb Krajina. It can be seen that such crimes were not committed by state structures. On the contrary, the man was arrested and prosecuted. You cannot really shift the blame now to the government of the Republic of the Serb Krajina in terms of something that was committed by an individual. Had we organised that, then the perpetrator would have been hidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, where does it say in the document that the person was convicted or even indicted? Does it say that anywhere in that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, in the archives of the Republic of Serb Krajina, all of that exists. It was all seized and taken to Zagreb. This is one of the very few documents that was kept from the area that you're interested in. You've just started reading about the eastern part of the Krajina now. A man was convicted to several years in prison, a man who killed several Croats and one or two Hungarians, if I'm not mistaken. He was tried by the court of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. Due to our lack of archives now, I cannot bring you these documents, and I cannot bring you the judgement, but you can obtain all of that in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, what sentence did this man get? How -- for what was he convicted? Do you know that? Do you know that this report really resulted in a conviction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or in a trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. The Republic of the Serb Krajina functioned under those very difficult circumstances as a state. Nevertheless, there were many trials in Krajina. I cannot tell you about each and every individual trial; I dealt in other matters. But you have a minister of justice in Krajina. There was one, there was another one, there was yet a third one. You can call them and they can testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we can move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, during your testimony, you gave some population figures regarding Serbs in Croatia, and you said, inter alia, that according to your findings, 1 million Serbs lived in Croatia. And I would like to put to you some statistics. The first item is from the population statistics from the Croatian Statistical Institute, and it's in the Croatian language, but the population figures on the third page speak for themselves. So when they are on the ELMO, it's easy for everyone to understand. Could we please have the third page on the ELMO. It's the statistical report related to the census of 1991, and it also shows the other years. And we have here, when we look under Srbi, we have here the figures for the Serbs, and it says here for 1991, 581.000 and some -- and a few. And a little bit further down in relation to the percentages, it says Srbi, 12.2 per cent. That's actually the same figures that Mr. Kostic, who testified not long before you, also spoke about. How -- how -- your figure of 1 million Serbs, that is not reflected here, and you don't have any foundation for that; right? No official foundation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. I have to say that this is written in the Serbian language because the Croats are the only people in the world who have renounced their language. It hasn't been used for over a hundred years. This official data, as I said yesterday, is a falsification. It doesn't represent the Serb -- the figures accurately. Mario Nobilo, the Croatian ambassador, actually denied this information when he said that 251 -- 251.000 Serbs lived in the Krajina and another number lived somewhere else, and if you add all this up, you will find the correct number. I have also mentioned that the number of Siptars in Kosovo has been exaggerated by two and a half times. This was the Yugoslavia in which non-Serb cadres were preparing its dissolution. My name is Jarcevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to you also another source relating to the official source relating to the figures, and that is actually the Yugoslav survey from 1992 that was produced in the Statistical Institute in Belgrade. And please also put on the ELMO the second page of this document. As you can see, Mr. Jarcevic, we have that same figure for 1991 census for the Serbs, and the same percentage again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I do not trust these percentages. They were taken over from Croatia. As I said yesterday, at republican level, censuses were falsified by reducing the numbers of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about -- what about this publication? It's from an institute --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't trust it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's by an institute founded by the Assembly of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is information taken over from Zagreb. As for the information from Zagreb, I've already told you everything about it three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not asking you about that at the moment. I'm asking you about this document called the Yugoslav Survey, and I'd be grateful if you'd concentrate on that. Can you tell me why you don't trust this publication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that we in Knin looked at these figures and arrived at a number of Serbs amounting to a little over a million.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Jarcevic. That's a point about the accuracy of the figures. What is it you say makes you not trust this publication? Is it anything other than the inaccuracy you maintain in the figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you have understood me. We verified this information in Knin and arrived at other figures. Of course we don't have our archives now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask it differently: Do you know this publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any other reason for doubting that it's a genuine -- that it would make a genuine attempt to reflect statistics accurately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Statistical information in this publication is what it is, but I do not believe that the number of Serbs is the number published in this publication. I think I've been quite clear. I don't know what else to say. Just as I don't believe that 1.700.000 Siptars lived in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to you another statistic from that same Yugoslav Survey Institute situated in Belgrade, and now it is from 1997. And the second page, please. The second page of this report, statistical report. And it's about the structure of the -- and the numbers of the persons -- war affected persons by former place of residence. And I would like you to look at table V in the middle of that page 95, as it says. We have here from Croatia the persons affected by the war, and we have here a figure from the UNPAs of 284.007, and from other parts of Croatia of 52.992. Mr. Jarcevic, these figures have nothing to do with what you told us about; that is, 471.000 Serbs living in Croatian towns and 400.000 expelled of these. And -- yes. That's basically this. What you told us about who was expelled from the towns, it is not reflected in these figures here, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it is reflected in the document issued by Boutros Boutros-Ghali on the 15th of May. There is a document here, handed over by Mr. Milosevic, showing that only in Yugoslavia and the UN protected areas 251.000 Serbs were expelled. That's his figure, not mine. As for the figure of 471.000, that's the figure provided by the Croatian ambassador. I only noted those figures; they don't come from me. As for the statistical information published by Serbia or the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which is now the state of Serbia and Montenegro, the state union, don't trust those figures, because all those who in the meantime have taken Serbian and Montenegrin citizenship or gone to third countries were immediately erased from the lists of refugees. Last year in May, the Government of Republika Srpska in exile handed over a letter to President Kostunica, Tadic, and the speaker of parliament, asking for this practice to be stopped. Otherwise, no information will exist any longer about Croatia expelling anyone. This is the trap into which you have now fallen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just remind us of the document from Boutros Boutros-Ghali which you say support the figures that you gave. What document is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report by Boutros Boutros-Ghali to the Security Council of the 15th of May, 1993, and it relates to the period from 1990 to early 1993. In English, it's page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to determine what to do with this document from Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Mr. Kay? We should have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the paragraph of that document that you say supports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's on page 4 of the text in English, and Mr. Milosevic has the text in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I may be mistaken, but I don't see any figures of that kind in this report, and I ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. Page 4, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 16, I think, is -- of Exhibit 338. I think that's where we are, according to my notes, when the witness gave evidence that Serbs started to leave from 1990 and 271.000 [sic] Serbs had fled from the Krajina, as noted in the UN Secretary-General's report of May 1993. At that stage in his evidence, he was dealing with Exhibit 338, tab 16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's tab 16?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, tab 16, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour in tab 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apparently it's tab 16, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's also -- I just found it also in tab 18. It's paragraph 10, and we find in this paragraph 10 also the figures of people fleeing to Serbia, and it's named here -- it's said 251.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jarcevic, these figures that are in that report, they actually match the findings of the Yugoslav Survey Institute. They also mention here 284.000 from the UNPAs, and 52.000 from the other parts. And if you look on the next page, the next page, this institute actually looks even more closely at these population moves, and you find here a table VI where it is divided according to years, and the years 1991, 1992, and 1993, are selected here as well as the year 1995. And you see that these figures are much, much lower than what you claim. Can you help us with that? And it's now a Yugoslav institute controlled by the Yugoslav state. It's nothing to do with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I have told you what the practice was. Anyone who took the citizenship of Serbia and Montenegro was no longer considered a refugee. Tens of thousands of people who at the time of this census were there went to foreign countries, such as Canada, Australia, and so on. None of these countries gave us the information we asked for in 1993. The number of people who fled to those countries is not less than the numbers who fled to Serbia. You don't have those figures, just as I never had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
