utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, this is a table -- both tables deal not with refugees but war affected persons by former place of residence. It's not just refugees. It's -- that's at least my understanding of this report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I haven't invented anything. I put forward two figures; the one provide by the Croatian Ambassador Nobilo whose document I don't have because it was seized by the Croatian police, and the Ghali report. If 251.000 Serbs were expelled from two areas which were suffering from sanctions, where there were no jobs and no possibility of new life, how many people then fled to countries which were providing better conditions and which were issuing visas to such people in those years with a very short and simple procedure? Then you can imagine the extent of the crimes against the Serbs in Croatia if you consider all these other aspects that are not contained in the document you are showing us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Jarcevic, do you accept that the data that are compiled here in this Yugoslav survey are actually prepared by the official bodies of the Yugoslav state, and they're acting according to the guidelines for preparing statistics? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I do not accept that this information contains all the facts about the Serb people expelled from Croatia. It doesn't mention the Serbs who fled to Canada, for example. That's why these figures cannot represent the whole issue of Serbs from Croatia. Ask Australia, Canada, the USA, Germany. As I said yesterday, the Germans said they would not forcibly send those Serbs back to Croatia, but they regretted the fact that they had the greatest expenses and costs in Europe because of these refugees, and this information is not contained here. I can't be any clearer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, are you aware that the state commission that prepares the census and that actually reviews the results, that this commission in Belgrade monitors the taking of the censuses in the -- all through Yugoslavia? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am, madam, but I've told you what methods they used. Anyone who took citizenship, and many were forced to do so, were no longer -- was no longer included in the figures you are reading out. And the same goes for third countries. While I don't have the right to ask you questions, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I obviously didn't make myself understood. I was now referring to the census data in general that we spoke about before we came to these other figures. The ones for the survey in 1991, were you aware that the state commission monitored -- from Belgrade, monitored the census-taking throughout the former Yugoslavia and thus the Croatian government or, rather, officials acted accordingly? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, madam, but the Yugoslav organs did not monitor anything in other republics. They simply took for granted what the republican statistical organisations provided them with.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender those three documents into evidence, because the witness has dealt with it -- with them and knows about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they're admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you also dealt with the document tab 13 of the Defence exhibit. Can we please have it again on the ELMO. That was the document related to Marica Varicak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Varicak.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you give the documents a number, please, those just admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: From the Croatian Statistical Institute for 1991 will be Exhibit 956. The extract from the Yugoslav Survey for 1992 will be Exhibit 957. And the extract from the Yugoslav Survey for 1997 will be 958.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, looking at Defence Exhibit 338, tab 13, that's now on the ELMO, and we don't have a translation, but is it correct that nowhere in this document there is an indication that the 21 incidents of explosions or the 381 incidents from 1991 on explosions and 673 incidents of 1992, nowhere in this document is a reference that the victims or the property -- that the owners of the property were Serbs; right? There's no indication here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I expressed my opinion about this yesterday. Let me just tell you that Marica Varicak is a Serb from Lika. This is an area that was part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. She resided in Zadar, and she was one of the 28.000 Serbs expelled from that town. This document was used during court proceedings to demonstrate that Serb houses were demolished. Marica Varicak --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat what you have told us about the case of Marica Varicak. Nowhere in this document, in this, except for the head Marica Varicak, is the ethnicity of the owner mentioned of any of these other incidents; correct? It doesn't say in these two paragraphs dealing with the figures of 21, 318 [sic], or 673, it doesn't mention the ethnicity of the owners; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course they're not mentioned. This area was controlled by the Croats. We won't conclude that it was Croatian houses that were demolished. It was only Serb houses that were demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In that municipality of Zadar, there are also the villages Skabrnja and Nadin; correct? They were part of Zadar municipality, and they could be in that figures, too; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't answer that question. The organ that issued this document would most probably be able to tell you. Among these incidents, there may have been Croatian buildings, but they were mainly in Zadar. Zadar was one of the towns that was destroyed in Croatia mainly because companies and Serb houses dominated -- predominated in the centre of Zadar. A year later, there was only grass growing there, as if a park had been planned there. I have a friend who had a house in Zadar, and he says he now has an English lawn on the site of his house. I cannot tell you whether this includes areas which were partly in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, because as you know, in 1993, on the 22nd of January, the Croats perpetrated an aggression there, and then they burnt and destroyed --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We are digressing again from the issue we are talking about. This is a document related to these incidents of explosion and damage in the municipality of Zadar, and I asked you whether Skabrnja and Nadin would be included, and your answer, if I understand you correctly, is yes, you wouldn't know that. Just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't know, because this was issued for more than one court proceeding, and I was not able to know what these court proceedings were about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Zadar was also shelled by the JNA; correct? And so damages could also be caused by this shelling, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't say anything about shelling here. It only speaks of fires and explosions. Explosions, well, bombs have to be planted. I don't think that shelling can be described as explosions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But shelling can actually cause fire; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, fires, yes, but not explosive -- not shelling. Explosives planted by hand. I'm not a strategic expert or a soldier, but my general education allows me to make that kind of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you got aware at some point in time of the killing of about 260 people from the Vukovar Hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, madam. And I'd like us to talk about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You actually wrote a letter to the Mothers of Vukovar, Association of Mothers of Vukovar, and I would like to put this letter to you and to everyone else. Mr. Jarcevic, is this your letter that you wrote to the Association Vukovar Mothers in relation to the missing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the missing persons, yes, this is a letter that we sent from Zagreb when we were negotiating, just before the agreement of the 29th of March, 1994, was signed. And I took part in drafting the letter, although somebody else signed in my place, but I can give you a sample of my signature if need be. The mothers asked whether in Serbia there were any detained Croatian soldiers, and by this we told them that in Serbia, or in Yugoslavia, there were no prisoners, no people who were -- had been taken prisoner, and if there were any, we would help them to have them freed. We did not speak about people who -- any people who were killed or buried in the famous or infamous mass grave at Ovcara, but we can discuss that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jasarevic -- Jarcevic, sorry. Mr. Jarcevic, you knew that the mothers of Vukovar were actually looking for the missing, and you did not indicate in this letter that there was a mass grave. This is a letter from 1994, and you knew at that time, you were aware that there was a mass grave at Ovcara, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's an excellent question, madam. The Croatian government and Security Council rejected our proposal in 1993 to dig up Ovcara and to identify the bodies. And this rejection of that proposal is contained in a letter from the High Commissioner of Canada to the UN, William Fenrick, to the Security Council. I can tell you of the correspondence that we had with him over a six-month period. I was the man who in 1993, sometime in May, unless I'm very much mistaken, offered to dig up Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, let's go through these step-by-step. We heard evidence from Professor Dr. Strinovic, and it's transcript page 17938 and 17038. He mentioned that the first gravesite was actually discovered in Ovcara in 1992. And he further told us that the exhumations started in 1993, but that the exhumations were stopped by the Serb side and could only conclude in 1996. Is he correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct at all. There's a Security Council letter addressed to Prime Minister Bjegovic, which states that there would be no digging up in Ovcara, according to plan, or in Marino Selo, which are Serb graves, because there is no money in the Security Council to do so. That is literally what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Is it correct that the first trace of the gravesite was discovered in 1992? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I had a meeting with William Fenrick in the Yugoslavia Hotel in Belgrade, the fact is that before that year 1993, Fenrick had information about that mass grave and he was astounded when I told him, without consulting the head of state who was from the area, so without consulting the Prime Minister, that I guaranteed the digging up of the mass grave, and at that point in time he just couldn't believe it. I confirmed this to him in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to return now to the Exhibit 771. That's the Security Council report of 7th of November, 1992. And please put on the ELMO paragraph 86.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, just look at the ELMO where there is said that: "... the forensic expert accompanying the Special Rapporteur on his second mission located a potential mass gravesite approximately 2 kilometres south-east of the farming village of Ovcara ..." The grave is then described a little bit more, and also the -- the consideration that it may be the disappeared from the Vukovar Hospital. And there is also mention that the Special Rapporteur had requested that UNPROFOR provide round-the-clock protection of the gravesite, and there is also mention that the Special Rapporteur had informed the commission of experts recently about this. So it was actually the UN who discovered the mass grave and then guarded it and informed Mr. Fenrick or the commission of experts. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick came to see me to ask the government of the Republika Srpska Krajina permission to dig up the grave, and I granted that permission straight away. I think I made myself clear. But let me repeat for a third time: We asked as a reciprocation that the graves of the Serbs be dig out in Marino Selo, Marin's Village, in Slavonia, and he didn't adhere to that promise, and I'll ask -- explain why.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me put what Mr. Fenrick actually declared publicly to you. And it's an exhibit not yet in this case. It's a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just was reminded that the letter from Mothers of Vukovar, the answer, should be exhibited, his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 959.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just for the usher, it is the page --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just so to explain to you, Mr. Jarcevic, it is a cable with attachments from the UN related to the Ovcara gravesite from the 25th of February, 1995. In this cable is included an interoffice memorandum about how the negotiations were conducted, and actually on page 2 of that memorandum there is mentioned the discussions that were held with you in 1993. It says here -- it starts with -- when I look at the first, at the interoffice memorandum, it says on the first page, last line: "The investigation had been on the agenda of the commission of experts since late 1992." Then it is mentioned that they took -- they undertook detailed preparation to excavate the site between December 1992 and September 1993. The preparation included obtaining all assurances on the 23rd of April, 1993, from Mr. Jarcevic, the foreign minister. Is that how you remember it too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the Yugoslavia Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here in that same paragraph: "After the written authorisation had been received, the commission sent the 60-strong excavation team to the former Yugoslavia. Subsequently, during October 1993, the local authorities denied knowledge of the Knin authorisation and became increasingly obstructive ..." It's not money missing at the UN side. It is the local authorities obstructing the work of the commission. Can you help us with that? Why were they opposed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this is the first time I'm hearing this piece of information. I never heard of anything like this before, and it cannot be correct at all. Even if somebody did obstruct on the part of the local authorities, the government of Srpska Krajina would have to have been informed about it, because I'm quite sure that that what Fenrick promised me was never brought to completion. And there are several letters that we have kept in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and I think that President Milosevic's associates do in fact have a letter where it says that because of the lack of money, they would be putting a stop to the digging up of both localities, both sites. And we proposed our own pathologist. They never called him to join the team, although they did record his name. His name was Zeljko Karan and he was from Banja Luka, pathologist from Banja Luka. I can go on if you're interested in hearing more about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'd like to go with you further through this memorandum of the UN in relation how the exhumation went along. And it says here in the next paragraph: "On 15 and 16 October 1993, the Commission received 'Decrees' from Knin authorising the excavation provided that the medico-legal examination did not take place in Croatia," and the UN agreed to this. Then it continues: "On the 22 October 1993, Colonel Milanovic informed the commission that despite all previous written assurances, the excavation was to be postponed until an overall political solution had been found to the situation in the former Yugoslavia." Now, tell me, why would you need to have a political solution to excavate a gravesite? Why was that suddenly a condition?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that this is the first time I hear of this. And why would a letter coming from Fenrick to the government of the Srpska Krajina, why did it not contain this fact? We would certainly have reacted. So in his letter it says because of a lack of money, there will not be the digging up of both gravesites. And I think that this Court will receive a letter, will be shown a letter to that effect. I'll do my best to find it. Now, Bastion [phoen], who was the deputy of Mr. Fenrick, didn't want to go to Belgrade and interview a man who was the sole survivor of the execution in Marino Selo. He said he wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who has this letter, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a copy of it at home, and I will send the letter to you at the first -- earliest opportunity. The letter is from Fenrick to the Prime Minister Bjegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have more documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't send to it to me. Send it to the accused or his associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Among those documents that I have here related to Ovcara there is no such letter that you mentioned but there is a press release. And please could you put the press release of the 2nd of November - it's enclosure number 3 - on the ELMO. And it is actually, according to this document, it seems to come from Mr. Fenrick. And he explains how -- how he prepared for the execution of the excavation and how he got first the permits to do that. And then he says on the second page of this press release: "However, in October 1993, after the arrival in the former Yugoslavia of the persons mentioned above, some local representatives of the Knin administration in the Ovcara area began to create obstacles for the Commission's project, in particular, Colonel Milanovic." And he also continues to write on the next page that: "The Commission, however, firmly believes that the truth about the Ovcara mass grave is impossible to hide regardless of what obstacles are currently put in the way of the investigation. "The Commission further deplores this delay for humanitarian reasons since the identification of the remains would alleviate the anxieties of the families of disappeared persons." And he says also in the last line that: "... the attitude of the Government of Croatia was positive and helpful." He does not mention any problems with money, and he does also not mention any reciprocity with the exhumations in Ovcara and the other gravesites; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised to hear that, because along with this fact or information that he hasn't got enough money, he said that the commission would be disbanded, and that's what happened, unless I'm mistaken, at the beginning of 1994. He just said orally that the Tribunal in The Hague would continue what they should have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we look at enclosure number 4. That's indeed a letter from you of the 6th November 1993, and it relates, obviously, to the press release of Mr. Fenrick. And you say here in paragraph 2: "The RSK has granted permission for the Ovcara venture on condition that a concurrent excavation of mass graves in Marino Selo and Pakrakca Poljana in Western Slavonia was also implemented in that -- in the presence of the team of Krajina forensics." You bring forward here a reciprocity between excavation in two mass graves. That's not mentioned in any of the documents by the UN. Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff claims is not correct. It's not correct that the United Nations do not mention in any of the documents, do not mention this. So she's asking the witness the wrong question, an incorrect question, because in the memorandum that she quoted a moment ago, UNPROFOR interoffice memorandum that she quoted from a moment ago, just one paragraph lower down from the paragraph she quoted from, and she was quoting from page 2, a paragraph beginning with, "On the 15th and 16th of October 1993, the commission ..." et cetera, et cetera, received a decree from Knin. In the following paragraph it already says this in the document, the UN document. It says that Jarcevic sent a letter to Fenrick in which it says, and you can read it for yourselves, Jarcevic's quotation: "I must most strongly remind you that the government of RSK has granted permission for Ovcara venture on condition that a concurrent excavation of mass graves in Marino Selo and Pakracka Poljana (Western Slavonia within Sector West, where he alleges 2.500 Serb bodies) were also implemented, and in the [In English] ... presence of a team of Krajina forensic experts. It was naturally agreed that a team of Croatian forensic experts should be present at Ovcara." [Interpretation] So that we can see clearly that in the UN document mention is in fact made of what in her question Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff says is not mentioned and she's putting that to Mr. Jarcevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this -- this first document that Mr. Milosevic just referred to, that's the summary of the events, and I was not completing this summary of events but took actually the letters that we had attached to. So what they are actually referring to is just the letter that I just put to Mr. Jarcevic and ask him why did he, in November 1993, for the first time mention that there was an agreement. And that's exactly what is mentioned in this report here, that he -- or on the 6th November, as it says here, wrote this letter. And in the -- it's -- in the report summarising what was going on, it says actually -- a comment of the author of the report is that he has no means verifying the accuracy of the statements of Mr. Jarcevic in his letter. And I was just putting this to Mr. Jarcevic. I asked him why on the 6th of November did he bring this forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, those conditions were mentioned in the Yugoslavia Hotel when I first met Fenrick, our first meeting. He told us orally that he accepted the conditions, and you know that there are oral agreements which have as much value as written agreements do, and I'm quite certain that we are lacking documents here in which that is stated before the date that you're specifying. Let me repeat that our archives were seized by the Croatian police. However, the documents can be found, I'm sure, in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, Mr. Fenrick, in his press release of the 2nd of November, does not mention this fact, but let me just ask you this: Why do you insist on a degree of reciprocity in the investigation of mass graves? What does one mass grave have to do with the other?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. We informed Mr. Fenrick of about 70 mass graves of Serbs in Knin. I'm sorry, I meant to say in Croatia. So it's quite logical that the United Nations do not have the right to deal with the crimes of just one party, one side. They have to look at the crimes of both sides, to care about them. And so Fenrick, with an explanation from our part, said all right, we're going to dig up for the moment just this one in Western Slavonia. And I can tell you also what Fenrick also explained to us later on, what he told us later. He said he found empty graves with no bodies after a certain time had passed and when the commission was about to be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender these documents, this group of documents into evidence. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that there was a recommendation in the end that the ICTY should consider approaching the Croatian government and Knin authorities with a view to having the two exhumations carried out. Did the Office of the Prosecutor follow that up?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know that, Your Honour. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You surely understand the point the witness is making about even-handed investigation, and I just wondered if that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution did not -- did usually ask other authorities to do such things, and I'm not aware that these other mass graves -- these other graves were done by the commission of expert. I will try to find an answer to that, Your Honour, but at the moment, off the top of my head, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 960.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you spoke about your participation in negotiations with the Croatian authorities, and you actually referred mostly to these global political questions. However, you also had negotiations on, as I see -- I have here a press release from the 15th of December, 1992, and it just refers to the fact that the Croatian government has proposed through UNPROFOR the normalisation of relations with the Republic of Serbian Krajina related to the opening of roads, establishing of rail transport, power plants, bridges, and those kind of things. Negotiation on these more practical and economical facts took matters -- took the place, right, of what their proposal, the Croats' proposal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the contents of this was something that all the meetings dealt with, whether directly with the Croatian delegation or with the mediators like Thornberry, but on our side we asked that roads be opened from Slovenia to Hungary. We wanted an exit into the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Could this be exhibited, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 961.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before we go into a few very specific negotiations, I would like to put to you something that you said at that time about your counterpart on the Croatian side, and first of all I would like to put to you an exhibit from the newspaper Glas Srpski of the 14th and 15th January 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's called "Reaction of Slobodan Jarcevic, RSK Minister of Foreign Affairs." And the headline is "Danger for the RSK." And it says here in the first point under the headline, it says: "I hope the world will realise that all the evil that has come upon the former Yugoslavia comes from Croatia and the artificial Muslim creation, which both initiated the war in an attempt to destroy the Serbian people." That was your view at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a little but further down here, it says: "Jarcevic reiterated the view that a 'monster state,' which once already existed, was again being created in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." What do you mean by "monster state that already -- that once already existed"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is very simple, madam: It cannot have a joint coat of arms, a joint language, a common flag, and I don't know what else you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say a little bit further down: "Judging by all, the form of federation or confederation with Croatia is being envisaged for RSK which is unacceptable for us." So you actually always strived for statehood of the RSK and the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our ultimate objective because of our historical experience. As for the Croatian proposals, as I've said, it only had to do with two towns and their surroundings. And as I said, we always rejected that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to go now to another of --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be exhibited? I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And by the way, I forgot to ask you: You mentioned the Muslims being an artificial -- Muslim nation being an artificial creation. Do you still think that? Is that still your point of view?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. All Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina are ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have here another newspaper article, also from Glas Srpski from 15 February 1993, and it has the headline: "Forbidden words: 'Co-existence' and Autonomy!" "Co-existence" is in converted commas, and it's actually the Croatian word for co-existence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are wrong, madam. That is a Serb word. The Croatian language hasn't been used for the past 100 years. It was called the Kajkavian dialect in scholarly circuits, but that was a mistake and they just took for state use a pure language, the pure Serbian language, and they've spoiled it a bit in order to give the expression of the existence of two languages. Croatian is the only language which is not under the protection of UNESCO, although UNESCO takes care of 6.000 different languages in the world that are about to become extinct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, this is a -- actually the opinion or report about a delegation of the RSK, and it's mentioned who was part of it, and I see your name here, too, and it says here on -- I have -- it's in the last column. It's the last column in the Serbian, and in the English it's on the second page, the top paragraph. It says here: "... we have recently refuted Mr. Owen's statement that we are going to those talks for reasons of the establishment of some sort of 'co-existence' and autonomy of the Republic of Croatia. That is not why we are going there, and precisely those two words, 'co-existence' and autonomy, will be permanently banned during the negotiations!" Mr. Jarcevic, does it mean that those sayings were proposed to you, offered to you, co-existence and autonomy, and you didn't -- you rejected this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'm telling you for the fifth time: Co-existence and autonomy only in two towns, and that would escalate to totally senseless proportions in 1993. And the Z-4 plan in 1994 when for those two municipalities, two towns, they envisaged money, a flag, an army, a parliament, a coat of arms, and participation in the Croatian authorities. So two-thirds of the Republic of Serb Krajina would have been excluded. It would have automatically become part of Croatia and probably the inhabitants of those areas would have fared the same way as the inhabitants of Zagreb, Split, Dubrovnik and Sisak fared: They were all expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just another and the last quote from that period in relation to Croatia I would now like to put to you, and that's a letter that you wrote to Aleksa Buha from the RS, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Your Honour, could the previous article be exhibited, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 963, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have here -- Mr. Jarcevic, this is a letter that you wrote to Mr. Buha, and we have it translated. However, this letter was read out in an Assembly session of the 11th of September, 1993 in the Republika Srpska Assembly. Do you recall that you wrote such a letter to Mr. Buha and do you know that it was read out and applauded to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just want to quote one little section of it, and it is on --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just go ahead, bravely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's basically in the middle of your letter, and it says here -- it's on the bottom of first page, Your Honour, in the translation, last few lines: "We must not make the same mistake today as we did so many times before. Serbian Knights must be on Serbian borders. The villain, who was taught from his childhood to exterminate the Serbian people, must not step on Serbian land. Too much of our land was taken away from us during this century for us to be able to give up even one inch of it now." That's really a quite -- I would call this hate speech, or a very nasty propaganda remark, Mr. Jarcevic; glorifying the Serbs and demonising the Croats, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the genocide over the Serbs in the camps of death, how can you describe it in other terms? Try. Try for yourself. Tell us. 700.000 Serbs killed in the Jasenovac camp. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you were saying this, Mr. Jarcevic, you were saying this about the people you were supposed to negotiate an agreement with. How can you as a foreign minister use such a language? That cannot allow for results in negotiations, can it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said does not look like hate speech at all. If you wish, I can paraphrase something that was stated by the Croats and what they even published in newspapers for children, and that is going to horrify you. Here I'm talking about Serb land that has to be in a Serb country, and that is the view I espouse to the present day, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Serbian borders. You speak about the Serbian borders. Where would they be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I know that this is a provocative question. You think that I shall not agree to say that Serb borders are where the Serb language is spoken and where the Serb people live and where half of the Serbs were exterminated, like in Kordun, from 1941 to 1945. Not a single country has the right to take up a territory where it committed genocide, Croatia least of all. And they hold these lands until the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- Mr. Jarcevic, can I ask you a quite different question about the same document. Assuming that you've finished with it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look much nearer the beginning, about ten lines into the letter, certainly in the English version, you write: "Nobody questions the noble intention of the Serbian army, which wants to put a stop to wartime looters." Then a little below that you talk about something having an impact on the weakening of the spirit and faith in Serbian arms and Serbian state, and then something's missing. And then go down about another ten lines, and you say: "Statesmen and journalists in the world write only about the rebellion of the Serbian army in Banja Luka ..." What did you mean to refer to by the Serbian army and Serbian arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb army is called the Serb army to this day in Republika Srpska. This was an event that I didn't even understand at that time. There was a conflict between the leaders of Republika Srpska and even military officers. I wrote a letter, and I requested that this be pacified, that a solution be found, because everybody was talking about it. And I was referring then to the Serbs expelled from Croatia, that nobody was taking care of them, that nobody was writing about them, and we are surprised how come it is only today that this is being talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if that's really what you're saying, Mr. Jarcevic. Just go back to near the beginning again, just before the first reference I gave you. You say: "The Serbian people in Krajina need help. Every Serb must provide it. I write this letter to you so that you can communicate to the officers and soldiers in Banja Luka that the Serbian people face a possible defeat." Now, who do you mean by "the officers and soldiers in Banja Luka"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said a few moments ago that there was a conflict in the top echelons of the military, in the corps that was stationed in Banja Luka. I don't know about the details, I don't know about the reasons, but it was unpleasant to read about that in the world media when the problems of the Serb people were something completely different rather than mutual squabbling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. May I just add something? When I said that Krajina was in danger, I was actually alluding to the fact that there is not a single people in the world, if they were to be attacked, say, from the north, that the people living in the south would say, "Do we care about our people in the north?" No way. And that is the kind of thing that was being expected, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I -- I would like this to be -- I would like to tender this into evidence, this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the negotiations, I only want briefly to touch on the negotiations in Norway, Mr. Jarcevic, and I would like to quote from what Mr. Vollebaek actually told the Court on the 8th of July, 2002, pages 7636 through to 7638. He actually -- as he said, you said you allowed for the possibility that he was in contact with Mr. Milosevic, and he actually told us about a meeting that he had in relation to the preparation of the negotiations in Norway, and he actually met Mr. Milosevic, and he said the following: "And I asked for his help, and he said that he would assist me because he felt that it would be difficult for the Croats to fight two fronts at the same time, and according to him it was more important to fight the Muslims than the Serbs. The Croats should be able to fight the Muslims, and in order for the Croats to fight the Muslims, the Serbs should kind of step back and let the Croats fight the Muslims." Did Mr. Milosevic express this view not only to Vollebaek but also to the delegation or members of the delegation of the RSK? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. Milosevic, he never spoke to me or to other people when I was present about where the Serbs should be in the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, and I'm surprised that Vollebaek is confusing that subject with this other subject at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vollebaek, on page 7638, says the following, and it's again -- it's still on the meeting with Mr. Milosevic. He says: "And then in order to let the Croats concentrate, so to say, on the Muslims, he - Milosevic - would ask the government in Knin to participate in the talks that we were going to have in Norway and then for the time being at least not pursue military activities." This is what he said he would do, Mr. Jarcevic, and this is actually what Mr. Lazarevic told us about when he testified and spoke about the meeting that Hadzic and this other Rakic had with Milosevic. Do you still deny that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this statement of Vollebaek's is more than naive. If the Croats had attached that kind of importance to these negotiations, they would have signed the agreement. But they refused it. What does that mean, being in Norway for two days, about ten 10 people from one side and ten people from the other side? Did they win any battle against the Muslims by going to Norway? None of this is correct, because the negotiations had nothing whatsoever to do with the Muslim-Croat conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, do you allow for the possibility that Mr. Milosevic said such things to Mr. Vollebaek at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to engage in guesswork, madam. Please free me from that kind of responsibility. I can just say, as far as Vollebaek is concerned, that he is a man who is not to be trusted. I'm just going to tell you about another particular case which will make you believe what I said about that man's character. If you wish, I will tell you about this. He stole my bag at the airport. If you wish, I can bring you an interview about that that was published in a magazine after we returned. I threatened to take him to court, and he brought my bag from Zagreb, and he never even met me, just brought the bag and left it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to continue to quote from that same page, and this is something that Mr. Vollebaek tells the Court at that time and which is actually confirming again what Mr. Lazarevic said. "Well, we were under the impression that the government in Knin was heavily supported, strongly supported, by the government in Belgrade and then, in casu, then President Milosevic. We knew that members of the Knin government went to Belgrade very often, and we thought and presumed that President Milosevic had strong influence on the government in Knin. And since the representatives of the Knin government then went to Norway for these talks, later on I was strengthened in my belief that there was an influence from Belgrade on the government of Knin." Do you deny that there was such an influence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an influence in terms of peace. We heard that. He certainly advised us in that direction; peace, not war. As for these talks of theirs, I repeat that I am not aware of any such thing. Nothing like that was conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just come in on one matter? It would certainly help the Defence if a question such as that could be put in the framework of the timing of the indictment from August 1991 to June 1992. The context of Mr. Vollebaek's evidence and that of Lazarevic in relation to period is obviously very important, but a distinction may well have to be made in terms of period for the counts of the indictment, and that is something that I raise because it is of importance to the Defence to know exactly what evidence is being relied upon in the cross-examination of a witness, and to what effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what period are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the period of 1993. There is no doubt about that. I mean -- and I mean I'm a little bit surprised about this remark, because we are dealing with three indictments covering that whole period but we are not having the witness coming three times. He is here now, and we will address everything that relates to all three indictments with the witness. This is what I'm talking about, and if the case of the Prosecution is that Mr. Milosevic had actually a strong grip on the leadership of the Republika Srpska Krajina from 1990 onwards, this is of course important that it continued to be like this throughout the whole period until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just clarify the particular period in relation to the evidence when you ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it was actually -- we had discussed the Norway negotiation in 1993. That's why I didn't give -- bring the witness through all these remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely sure I follow your point about the link between or among the three indictments, because the Bosnian indictment doesn't include the witnesses that -- or the personnel we've principally been concerned about, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As part of the joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, the JCE members are actually the same except for that additional ones come into the play, that is Mr. -- General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. It's the same JCE, just evolving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time to take the break. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just as an example: There is no reference to Babic in the Bosnian indictment, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. That's correct, Your Honour, because Babic was ousted in 1991 because he didn't, according to our evidence, obey Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No reference to Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Bulatovic? I'm not sure. I think Bulatovic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are, I would suggest, differences. No reference to Seselj. Oh, yes, there is. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution is that it is one JCE evolving over times when personnel was ousted or -- or left this JCE for other reasons. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, did you also take part in negotiations in 1995 with Ambassador Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, when in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In -- in the negotiations related to the Z-4 plan up to May 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I said that I didn't, and I also explained in what situation and at what time that plan was offered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I don't need to ask these questions. You were relieved from your position as the foreign minister of the RSK when -- when exactly and why?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was in April 1994, as Dr. Milan Babic had won the majority in parliament. He was appointed minister of foreign affairs, and I handed over my duty to him in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. Mr. Jarcevic, I have here a document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have here a document that appoints you to a position. Just -- just briefly, according to a decision of the 2nd of May, 1994, Mr. Milan Martic appoints you to his advisor for foreign policy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me to take up that job, explaining that he knew Dr. Babic and that he would do nothing in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Therefore, he asked me to do part of the affairs in -- with foreign countries as part of his office. And as you can see, I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could that be accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 965.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Jarcevic, when you took up this position, did you then move to Knin or did you continue to be in Belgrade and in that office of the RSK in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in Belgrade. I changed offices because President Martic had his own office about six kilometres away from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This was all in Belgrade. And that was the distance, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We had previously mentioned that the negotiations with the Croats, when they started in 1992 and throughout the -- when they lasted, also included economic agreements, and they actually did result in some improvements; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a very small extent, madam, because the Croats did not want to use the Maslenica bridge as we offered them before my arrival. I'm referring to the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in 1992. And it's interesting to note that on the 22nd of January, 1993, these negotiations were to continue, and two commissions were to meet. I don't know in what village exactly, in Ravni Kotari, and as usual, on that day Croatia perpetrated an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, the -- as a result of these negotiations, the highway Zagreb-Belgrade was opened in winter 1994, was it -- was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the results that seemed to promise agreement could be reached in other areas as well. Krajina was whole-heartedly in favour of it. I know that. The Prime Minister at the time was Mr. Nikolic, and Rade Tanga was the minister of defence. He was the first to drive down the motorway from Western Slavonia to Vukovar through Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this -- this highway was actually closed in 1995 three times by Mr. Milan Martic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know all the details about the temporary closure. You can't say it was closed or that the Republic of Srpska Krajina gave up on the agreement that he had signed. However, it was temporarily closed for not longer than 24 or 48 hours, I think. There was some kind of misunderstanding, but I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How come you can't? You don't know the details of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the details, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you accept that the attack on -- of the -- of the Croats in May 1995 on Western Slavonia was actually caused or triggered by the action of Milan Martic in relation to the highway? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't accept that. In March we had a document about the Croatian attack which was to take place on the 1st of May. We received it from the NATO headquarters in Brussels. Secretly, of course. We don't even know who sent it to us. And it was long before the highway was closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to play to the witness an intercept, a conversation. For the -- for the video booth, it's on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a precise reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For the interpreter, it's cassette number 15, side A, conversation between Mr. Milosevic and Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Let me tell you something. I've had telephone contacts both with the Russians and the Americans and with Akashi. They have stopped all combat activities. Celeketic even confirmed to Perisic that all combat activities had been stopped and that the Croats are not fighting any more. But they committed horrible crimes there. They shelled Zagreb, they shelled Sisak, Karlovac. They hit the children's hospital in Zagreb, butchered 15 children, and in general, everything that is happening is a result of Martic's wilful conduct. He closed the motorway on his own initiative three times, without the consent of the Krajina government, and even when we organised everything in order for it to reopen he said no, therefore, this other guy decided to drive him out. "He is crazy. He cannot get along with anybody at all. "I think that he needs to be replaced. Because of his wilful conduct that has caused so many casualties. "Well, I don't know how this thing is here any more ... I don't know that. Are you at work tomorrow? "I'm going to be at work. "I would call ... Do have anything planned? "Well, I'll probably have something, but do call. "I'll call around 1000 hours or 10.30. "But do call, I want to hear from you. "Okay. Good-bye. "Good-bye."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, this is Mr. Milosevic speaking to Goran Hadzic. Actually they are speaking about the shelling of Zagreb, and Mr. Milosevic is actually saying that Martic closed the motorway three times and that basically triggered the attack by the Croats. Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Croatia would have attacked us even had the highway not been closed. As I told you, we held in our hands the plan for the Croatian attack which we received from the NATO centre in Brussels. We don't know who sent it to us. I don't even know the people who brought it to us. The attack was planned to take place on the 1st of May. That's what the report said. And it was well known that the Serb leaders could not agree among themselves. Whatever conversation you intercept, you will hear things like this, even with other participants in the conversation. However, this particular conversation that you've asked me to comment on simply shows that the Serbs did not have a unified single plan in connection with the Republic of Srpska Krajina. The Prosecution, however, claims that it had and that the plan was to create some kind of Greater Serbia. This intercept demonstrates the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, Mr. Milosevic says here: "We organised everything in order to reopen the highway." "We"; that implies actually him being involved in that action. Do you know that he was doing this, that he was negotiating and preparing those things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interpret what Mr. Milosevic was saying. He's here. But I assume that when he uttered that sentence he was thinking of the Serbian nation as a whole, and all of us were holding some kind of office in that nation. I can assume, if you'll permit me to go on, that perhaps he was not aware of every detail that had to do with this conflict around the highway, especially if he was being informed by Mr. Hadzic who was having serious arguments with the head of state Milan Martic at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the reference to shelling of Zagreb, who is it suggested was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Milan Martic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He speaks about Milan Martic's wilful conduct, and the witness will probably confirm that Mr. Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb, Sisak, and Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it's a sin to mention those few rockets when thousands of rockets were fired at Serbian towns. I think I had a document in my hand showing that if Croatia attacked the Republic of Serbian Krajina, all military weapons were to be used against military facilities in Croatia. In Bosanska Gradiska, for instance, on the 1st of May the Croats bombarded the town in the neighbouring country and killed a lot of refugees who had fled from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, we do not have time to speak about the -- these other matters that you just referred to. We -- the question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I take it -- I take it, Mr. Jarcevic, that you have confirmed that Milan Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb, Sisak, and Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I guarantee that this was the strategy of the General Staff. What else can one do to an enemy but to retaliate with the same kind of means? I'm not saying that anyone, including Martic, issued an order that civilian targets be fired on. Were we supposed to throw chocolate at them?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this context, to make it even more clear for Your Honours I have another intercept that I would like to play. It's related again to the same time period, that is the 3rd of May, 1995, and this time it's again on Sanction. And for the interpreters, it's conversation -- conversation 68, Perisic and Milosevic talking. And we hear only two parts of this intercept, which is quite a lengthy one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I've just received written confirmation that Clinton personally talked to Tudjman. Of course privately over the telephone, and that he said he would make him pay if he continues with the animosities and start retreating there. Therefore, this has been confirmed. He received a bloody threat, but this Tihomir Dinic just told me that Stankov, this Stankov of ours, you know, he's now there with him in the Executive Committee, that he spoke with Martic. Martic told him that something was done again against the Serbs on Psunj Mountain and that that was why Akashi went there. He does not have any other choice but to shell Zagreb again, so please call Celeketic and draw his attention to it. You heard Tudjman last night. If they shell Zagreb, by any chance, he would not allow that retreat or anything else. He has 6.000 people in the encirclement and he is jerking around here by wanting to shell Zagreb, kill the civilians, and cause a reaction. That's number one. Call Celeketic and forbid him to -- and forbid him to do it and tell him not to even think about it. Akashi went there. Everything will be fixed and he should not do anything stupid. Due to the shelling of Zagreb, Martic was not in Zagreb the day before yesterday but he was in Zagreb only yesterday, so it is absolutely out of the question and he mustn't do that. Secondly ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And this continues, this intercept continues, and I would like to have just the next bit played, as indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Call Celeketic and forbid him to do that. Tell him not to even think about it. Akashi went there. Everything will be fixed and he should not do anything stupid. Due to the shelling of Zagreb, Martic was -- he was not in Zagreb the day before yesterday but only yesterday. So it is absolutely out of the question. He mustn't do that. Secondly, Martic said to this Pankov that he arranged yesterday with Karadzic in Banja Luka that these people from 'Republika Srpska' were to attack somewhere to take something. They don't mean Croats but to attack and take something there in their own battlefield. That would be very bad, because I have already received a report from the Greek. I will read it to you. Just a moment."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That should be -- can you please stop it? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Jarcevic, this is now a conversation on -- of the 3rd of May again, between Perisic and Milosevic, and actually Mr. Milosevic asked General Perisic to actually request Celeketic not to shell Zagreb. And did -- my question is: Did -- do you know whether the shelling of Zagreb then stopped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want me to say. You see, this conversation shows to what extent the people participating in it were advocating peace rather than war. It was Croatia that was waging war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer the question which was: Do you know whether the shelling of Zagreb then stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when it stopped, whether before or after this conversation, but it did stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, were you aware of the close relationship between the commanders of the VJ and the RSK -- the SVK, sorry, the army of the RSK. Were you aware of this, that one could basically order another?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe they could issue orders. They could take each other's opinion into account. For two reasons: Firstly, they had gone to school together and they knew each other; and secondly, they were members of the same nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I would like to put to you another --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I forgot to ask, could these two intercepts be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They were not exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, they are not yet exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they're admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first intercept between Mr. Milosevic and Goran Hadzic will be Exhibit 966. And the second, between Momcilo Perisic and Mr. Milosevic, will be Exhibit 967.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, would you know details about the military cooperation between the VJ and the SVK? Are you knowledgeable on this topic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a lot about it, but I can give you a conclusion. In every branch, we had relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. I don't want a conclusion. I actually was thinking about putting to you some documents, and I was just wondering whether you dealt with, in your office in Belgrade, whether as a foreign minister or in your capacity as advisor, with such military requests from the RSK organs to the VJ or Belgrade ministries. Would they come over your desk?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me take a look. I'll be quite sincere, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just wanted to avoid to put something to you that you never would have dealt with. Okay. The first document is -- it's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you know that I've never seen these documents, then don't show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is -- it's not an exhibit yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a request of the president of the RSK of the 21st of July, 1994, to the president of Yugoslavia and the president of Serbia and Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army in relation to recruitment and equipment for the SVK. First of all, do you know -- it's a request by Mr. Milan Martic, whose advisor you were at that time. Do you know about these requests that he made to the three organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just enter a correction? I was advisor for foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw materials of this sort, and I can tell you a little joke. I used to inquire with military personnel about the preparations for the defence of the Krajina, but the response I got was always the same: This is not like in communist times. Everybody should mind his own business, so you look after diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. And what it says here in this document, "The planned development and strengthening of the SVK is directly related to the supply of MTS by the VJ, as agreed." Could you help us with who agreed about what and when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who agreed on this, but by your leave, as I said, in every area, the two countries cooperated. The Republika Srpska Krajina, whether one wants to admit it or not, was a real state at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to page 10 of -- in the English, it also refers to the request for cluster rockets for the Orkan multiple-launch rocket systems. Do you know whether the RSK army received multiple-launch rocket systems from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I really don't know, but the officers always assured me that Krajina was well-armed. That was all the information I had. It was very general.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know that these cluster rockets were actually used for the shelling of Zagreb? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I really don't know anything about rockets, and to this day I'm not sure what a cluster bomb is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't know whether this line of questioning is productive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct. And I don't want to tender the document either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's just briefly move to the office of the RSK in Belgrade. The office that you worked in as a minister of foreign affairs, who owned this premises?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The owner of premises I think was the city of Belgrade, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to you Exhibit 352, tab 152. Mr. Jarcevic, it is an order by Chief of Staff of the VJ, General Zivota Panic. It is a military matter, and I only put it to you because the office of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Belgrade is mentioned here in point 4 of the first page of this document. Can we put it on the ELMO, the first page? It's an order directed to the accepting and initiating conscript soldiers into the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and it says in relation to the office of the RSK: "The assignment of the conscript soldiers will be performed by the Government's Office of the RSK in Belgrade ... and cooperation must be established with them." When it says here "must be established with them," is that you or who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. At that point in time it's me, and I'm telling you it's the 27th of January, five days after the bloody aggression of Croatia against the Republic of Srpska Krajina, which is why I gave an office to the minister for foreign affairs, so that Colonel Rade Tanga, who was later to become the minister of defence and director of the university, or the dean, could list the volunteers who were turning up from everywhere, even from abroad. We asked the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to assist us in recruiting citizens of the Republic of Srpska Krajina who wanted to volunteer to go to the borders of their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who exactly made this agreement? You and who else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just sent instructions to the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and I don't remember anything else. They phoned me up to tell me that I -- we could send our recruits, and it was in the office that the names were taken down, but nobody was forced and nobody in the federal organs of Yugoslavia went collecting up the young men and bringing them to my -- our office. It was all on a volunteer basis, regardless of what it says in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Another document, and that's related -- it's Exhibit 327, tab 9. And please put the first page on the ELMO. Mr. Jarcevic, it is a meeting held by the president of the -- hosted by -- sorry, hosted by the president of the Republic of Serbia of the 12th of November, 1992. I see that you are -- were not one of the participants in this meeting. However, did you learn about the meeting as you were the foreign minister at that time? Do you know about that meeting, about financing the police and the army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting is not one I knew about, but let me repeat: The two states did have relationships at all levels, in all fields. So you mustn't understand this as being financing by Yugoslavia of the army of Republika Srpska Krajina. The goods went on the markets of both countries, and finances were also calculated as they would be in either of the two states.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So I just would like to turn to the next exhibit. That's 327, tab 14. It is -- it's a letter to Milan Martic -- from -- by Milan Martic to Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Sainovic, and Zoran Sokolovic, and it's again about funds for the MUP of the RSK of the 28th of April, 1993. Were you aware about -- of this request and that the money actually came? It's about the salaries of the police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this document, I didn't know about it. I am seeing it for the first time. But in documents of this kind, you don't have all the facts relating to the economic relations of the two states. Serbia owed a lot to Krajina, and you won't be able to find this in this type of document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you were aware that the police in the RSK was financed by Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, madam. They were financed from the budget of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is here a letter, if you look at it, to the officials, including Mr. Milosevic, of the Republic of Serbia, and they ask for assistance in the payment of salaries. I understood that you said these were -- those kind of things were done.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, all I want to say is that the Republic of Serbia, or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, owed the Republic of Srpska Krajina certain monies which might have been used for these salaries. If you like, I can tell you about the economic situation and trade relations between the two countries and then you'll be able to understand that I'm speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, at the moment we don't have much time left, Mr. Jarcevic, so I can't really -- we can't go into these details. One -- one letter I would like to put to you, and that's actually something that you wrote and so you may perhaps know better about it. And it's not an exhibit yet, Your Honour. If you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my letter, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says -- it says here, "Jarcevic, counsellor to the president --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have received a letter that is addressed to Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, sir. Yes. You were given the wrong letter. I have skipped several documents and didn't tell Ms. Dicklich correctly. It is here a request or, rather, a letter that you write to Mr. Jovica Stanisic on the 24th of July, 1994. And it says here: "President Martic instructed me to organise the arrival of the Commission of the Union of Cossacks' armies of Russia and abroad, together with you." And can you -- you are writing here to Mr. Stanisic. Can you say why do that and what was agreed between Mr. Martic and Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, who else could I contact but the organs of the state on whose territory the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is active and the office of the Republic of Srpska Krajina? It is not us who can see to the arrival of foreigners at the airport of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That wasn't up to us. Nor can we issue orders to staff at the airport and the security staff as to what their job should be. So we asked the representative of the Republic of Serbia from the Ministry of the Interior to assist us and see that the delegation of Cossacks from Russia arrive in Belgrade, that we take it over, and take it to Krajina. Had we been in Paris, by any chance, then this letter would have been sent to the Ministry of the Interior of France.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here in this letter: "We need to have talks with them and to sign a contract on cooperation of RSK and RS with this organisation." So it was a joint action of the RSK and the RS, supported then by MUP Serbia? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not lend support. You can see he was surprised by my letter, but they didn't tell us -- or they didn't say that they weren't meddling in our internal affairs. They didn't say go ahead or don't go ahead. I visited Moscow myself and the Cossack organisation without a single man from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're not talking about Yugoslavia. We're talking about the MUP of Serbia. Stanisic would actually assist Mr. Milan Martic in all matters related to police; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking the question in an incorrect way. I say it is the authority of the MUP of Serbia in Belgrade at the airport. I have to respect that. Imagine if I went to France to Orly airport without asking anybody and then to invite guests there who might arrive and fly in without any visas, for that matter, whereas this is a very simple diplomatic step. There's nothing secret there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing puzzling.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- how long did the RSK office in Belgrade exist, or does it still exist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until -- well, the office of President Martic, until the 26th of February, 1996.
