At the present time, the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina has an office there and the exiled government, together with the exiled Assembly, is active, and we showed you yesterday support by 28 deputies from the parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe who signed a request by which Croatia should be returned to its two-nation state status. So that is a success scored by the government in exile of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Or, on the other hand, the understanding shown by the world towards the suffering that nobody had understood thus far.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My last question to you, Mr. Jarcevic: Are you a member of this RSK government in exile?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a counsellor or advisor in the government but no longer a minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions. Oh, yes. I would like to ask this last document that's the letter from Mr. Jarcevic be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let's take this in the right order. Mr. Jarcevic from the beginning Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you something about your activities linked to the suffering of the people in the western part of what was once Yugoslavia, and you explained that you were a member of the Association of Serbs from Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since at the beginning of your testimony when you introduced yourself you explained to us that you were one of the rare babies to have survived the Ustasha slaughter, and during that, was Bosnia-Herzegovina a component part of the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the Serb Muslims were -- were proclaimed the flower of the Muslim nation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the Croatian nation, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me: Was there a difference between the Ustashas' attitude toward Serbs, depending on territory, whether it was Bosnia or Herzegovina or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, equal treatment. And a few days ago I saw a document found in the archives of Sarajevo. It was an order by the State of Croatia to kill, first of all, people between the ages of 30 and 50 and then children up to the age of ten. I was in that category, the latter category, and it was just by chance that I happened to survive. Many of my friends say what a pity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time, in 1991, 2, and 3, when you became minister, did you differentiate with respect to the suffering of Serbs in Bosnia and in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the same, the intimations were the same as they were in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the next question Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you, and in presenting certain United Nations documents here, was linked to the alleged persecution of Croats in Serbia. Because you said that there was no such persecution, and you quite rightly said that, because this one case that happened in Hrtkovci seems to be played here again and again, brought up again and again. Now, in connection with that you were also asked something with respect to a document of some kind. You were shown it at the beginning. The 17th of November, 1992, was the date. A very long document. I'm not going to use it in its entirety. I'd just to highlight certain portions and ask you about them. Have you got the document in front of you? It is the 17th of November. It says: "Human rights questions: Human rights situation and reports of the special rapporteurs and representatives." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you mean a report of the United Nations on human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the United Nations report, I said at the outset. It's the thickest document that you were provided with and you were given it at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what are you asking about it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at paragraph 94, which was not quoted. You explained that the subject was incidents which were caused by the refugees from Croatia. That's what you've said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at what it says in paragraph 94. Do you have paragraph 94 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found 94, no. [In English] 94, find me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs are numbered in order. It's easy to find them, I believe. Have you found it now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Serbia and Montenegro received 500.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "[In English] It should also not be forgotten that Serbia and Montenegro have received some 500.000 refugees from Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Slovenia." [Interpretation] And then there's another line: "[In English] The economic sanctions imposed by the United Nations in accordance with its charter have also had effect upon the everyday life of people." [Interpretation] And so on. Now, in this report by the United Nations, could we see this figure of 500.000 refugees already at that time? The number included in the November report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might be allowed to add, at that point in time the United Nations are introducing the most terrible sanctions against Yugoslavia and the Republic of Srpska Krajina. And if I may state my own personal opinion, this is the dark side of our civilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you answer the question? Did you answer -- you have not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, yes. The president asked me what the situation was like with these 500.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at paragraph 123, point 123, which speaks of the following or, rather, it's about -- more about what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you. And you said that the refugees caused the incident. Was that common knowledge? That's my question to you. Was that known at the time to the international organisations and the UN? What does paragraph 123 state? "[In English] The outbreak of fighting in neighbouring parts of Croatia and the influx of Serbian refugees coincided with an increase in incidents of harassment and violence against non-Serbs in Vojvodina." [Interpretation] And then a few lines on they quote our government and say: "[In English] In recent special report to the human rights committee, the federal government, stated [no interpretation] Some of these people fleeing from conflict in the hope of saving their lives and those of their families have arrived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, bringing with them their weapons, resolve to set up a new home even if it means using force to achieve their aim at the expense of the people belonging to non-Serb nations -" [Interpretation] in bracket - "[In English] Croats and others, whom they regard as enemies simply because they do not belong to the Serb nation." [Interpretation] So that is a report by our government quoted here, and then we have a quotation or, rather, Hrtkovci are quoted, are mentioned, Hrtkovci. And four lines on, what does it say here? "[In English] The government indicates that the Serbian Ministry of the Interior has begun an inquiry to determine whether there was any complicity by local authorities in these events that large quantity of weapons and explosives have been seized and that a number of individuals have been charged with criminal offences, including homicide." [Interpretation] Do you know that that was the only killing then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really don't know how many killings there were, but this report is one I've never seen before, and I'm very happy to have confirmed what it says in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jarcevic, that the people who perpetrated the killing in Hrtkovci were arrested and taken to trial, that single killing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not my fault that I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's move on. You went on to answer questions put to you by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and quoted a document from which we can see that in Republika Srpska Krajina there was also persecution of individuals who had -- or prosecutions of individuals who had committed crimes against Croats. You quoted that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in that document that quoted, did it say that five Croats had been killed, as far as I remember - I haven't got the document in front of me - and that it also gave the name of the suspect who was arrested?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and information that he was apprehended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it stated that the man was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That he was apprehended by the Krajina authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then we had other examples?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So now, what do you know about this? Did the Republic of Srpska Krajina function as a state ruled by law and prosecuted crimes perpetrated on its territory without discrimination, and here we can say that it is prosecuting people for committing crimes against Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there were many similar cases. I can't quote them all now because, as I say, the archives are to be found in Zagreb today, so I can't look them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that they do have certain facts and figures that can be found, but anyway, Mr. Jarcevic, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff -- well, thank you for your answer, but Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff then challenged your assertions in connection with your findings and attitude and position in Krajina about the population structure there. I'm not going to use three documents, I'm just going to use the first document, which is the population census of households, apartments and so on of the Republican Institute for Statistics for Croatia, and the year is 1992. Please take up that document, have a look at the report. She showed you the third page of it, and the document has a total of three pages, in fact. You were shown page 3 where we can see the figures. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've received it. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at -- well, we can see the 48, 53, 61, 71, 81, and 91 population census.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And take a look here. In 1971, it has -- says 626.789 Serbs, and in 1991 5 -- 581.663.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, have a look at when this figure occurs in the 9 -- in the 1971 census and then in the 1981 census.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Follow that column for 1981. How many Yugoslavs were there that year? 379.000, and in the previous census there were only 84.000. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many Serbs declared themselves as Yugoslavs, and I've already stated that. About 80 per cent of them, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say? 80 per cent of Serbs declared themselves as Yugoslavs whereas they were Serbs; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the estimates. And many researchers in Belgrade agree with those estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we were to add that number to the 531.000 minus 20 per cent, that would make it about 831.000 Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said about a million.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do these figures indicate that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I'm sorry that they didn't believe me when I said it. I didn't know that I should do the calculations and sums as you've just done them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're just figures, nothing other than that here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said in general terms a million-plus Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff put on the overhead projector the document you provided about the police report from Zadar relating to the number of fires and explosions. I'm sure you'll remember. I won't have it placed on the overhead projector again. We've already had a look at it twice; when I presented it and when Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff presented it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know about a phenomenon that was termed the crystal night in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a pogrom of the Serbs similar to the one that took place in Zagreb, and I apologise to go back in history again, but it happened in 1902.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Milosevic [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, is it probable that those hundreds of explosions and houses, is it possible that it was the Serbs blowing up Croat houses, or was it destruction of Serb houses and fires and explosions blowing up Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since all -- it was only the Serbs that filed lawsuits for this there, might have been one or two against Croats in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, but for the most part these were Serb houses, Serb villas, Serb shops and other facilities and including fisheries, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop. The interpreter is asking you to slow down, but we're going to adjourn for today and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honours, just one -- one observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness, Ms. Mahon. There are no exhibits for her. The 65 ter summary is exiguous in the extreme. It says almost nothing. If there is any way that the accused, by providing an advance notice -- she's an English witness, so any notes that she and he have made will be in English, if there are any notes that can be provided so that we know the scope of her evidence, this would be of great assistance and would more likely guarantee her conclusion tomorrow so that there is no question of her coming back next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
